### Supporting basis

Your workload features high redundancy due to repeated JSON field names across 10 GB of logs, which heavily favors Zstandard’s dictionary compression capabilities. Although Zstandard level 3 is aggressive, it typically matches or beats gzip level 6 in speed while producing significantly smaller files, especially when a custom dictionary is generated from sample data. Gzip level 6 offers a reasonable balance but lacks the advanced LZ77 windowing and context mapping that Zstandard utilizes to exploit the repetitive structure of newline-delimited JSON. Since decompression occurs repeatedly, Zstandard’s superior decompression throughput is critical; it is multi-threaded by default and processes data faster than gzip’s single-threaded decompression. While zstd requires managing a dictionary for optimal results, the initial creation is a one-time cost. The trade-off favors zstd because the reduced storage size lowers I/O latency during frequent reads, and the faster decompression minimizes CPU bottleneck in downstream processing, whereas gzip’s smaller CPU overhead during compression is negligible given the single-thread constraint and vast scale of the archive operation.

### Recommendation

I recommend using Zstandard at compression level 3, provided you generate and embed a custom compression dictionary from a representative subset of your log data. This approach leverages the repetitive nature of JSON keys, drastically reducing the compressed archive size beyond what gzip can achieve, while maintaining exceptionally high decompression speeds. The marginal increase in CPU usage during the one-time compression phase is a worthwhile investment, as the resulting smaller file size and faster decompression will yield significant performance gains during the repeated read operations. If implementing dictionary generation is technically prohibitive, Zstandard level 3 still generally outperforms Gzip level 6 in decompression speed, making it the superior choice for your write-once, read-many workflow. Avoid Gzip only if legacy tooling constraints strictly prohibit Zstandard, as the benefits in throughput and space efficiency are substantial for this specific data profile.<|im_end|>
